Subject: Performance SLO qualification — Veridian Analytics (post-call recap)

Alex — great talking today. Quick recap from our perf/SLO discussion and proposed next steps so we stay aligned. TL;DR: we think we can hit your targets with a combination of continuous batching, prefix/KV caching, targeted quantization, and model-variant routing — SE (Dev) will validate with a perf run once we have sample payloads/traffic.

Key targets you called out on the call:
- Latency: 95th percentile end-to-end "response complete" latency <= 300 ms for non-streaming flows (goal). For streaming token-by-token scenarios, per-token latency target ~< 120–150 ms.
- Throughput: sustained ~3k requests/minute (50 rps avg) with bursts to ~10k req/min (~167 rps) for short periods.
- Concurrency: steady-state concurrency ~60 concurrent sessions, spike concurrency up to 200.
- Payloads: median prompt length ~250 tokens, 95th prompt length ~1,200 tokens. Average generated tokens per request ~80.

Cost target: you mentioned wanting to stay sub-$0.60 per 1k responses (ballpark) for the majority of production traffic — we flagged some tradeoffs below.

Primary cost/performance levers we discussed:
1) Continuous batching: small batching windows to aggregate requests across sessions while respecting per-request latency SLO (e.g., 10–30 ms micro-batching window). Helps amortize kernel overhead and increases GPU utilization.
2) Prefix & KV caching: if you have repeat or template-heavy prompts (sounds like you do for analytics summaries), caching the prompt prefix / KV cache across sessions can cut per-request compute substantially.
3) Quantization profiles: run the high-throughput endpoints on an aggressively quantized profile (Q4_0 / int8 where quality is acceptable) and route the fidelity-sensitive traffic to higher-precision variants.
4) Model variants & smart routing: 13B-quantized for high-throughput low-cost endpoints; 70B (or unquantized 70B-optimized) for high-quality bursts or edge cases. Automatic fallback if quality checks fail.
5) Autoscale & pre-warm: configure minimum reserved replicas during business hours to avoid cold-start latency spikes; leverage burst pools for predictable burst capacity.

Next steps (action owners / timing):
- Alex: share a sanitized sample of 1,000 representative requests + a 2-hour traffic trace (timestamps + payload sizes) by EOD Friday 3/19. This will let Dev run a realistic perf pass.
- Dev: will produce a perf test plan and recommended config (batching window, min replicas, model variant split, quantization profile) within 48 hours of getting traces.
- Marissa/Neha: send the MAP and SLO_calculator we shared on the call (attached) — will include cost estimates for the recommended config.

Attachments: 20260315-Veridian-MAP.pdf (mutual action plan), SLO_calculator.xlsx (config + cost calc).

If any of the numbers above are off, call it out — otherwise I’ll schedule a 30-min POC kickoff next week (Dev + Neha + your eng lead).

Thanks,
Marissa
Senior Solutions Lead | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai | (415) 555-0142

Note: We plan to validate with two perf profiles: 
A) high-throughput (quantized 13B) — aim for cost-efficient steady-state;
B) high-quality (70B or larger) — handle 5–10% of traffic or on-demand fallback.

2) Traffic shape: I can export a 2-hour trace of production-like synthetic traffic that matches our weekday morning spike and include p50/p95 prompt lengths. Will send by Fri 3/19 as requested.

4) Procurement: Jordan — FYI we may need a short statement of work for the POC and a rough pricing band to move procurement quicker.

Question for Dev: any red flags on supporting token streaming with continuous batching? Specifically: will batching introduce extra per-token latency or chunking artifacts for streaming consumers?

Hi Alex — short answers up-front, then recommended config: 

Q: Will continuous batching hurt streaming per-token latency?
A: Not if configured carefully. Redwood supports hybrid batching for streaming: micro-batches for request-level compute while still pushing tokens as soon as the runtime produces them. Key knobs: batching window (we typically start 10–30 ms), batch size cap, and per-request deadline.

Recommended starting config (to validate in perf run):
- Batching window: 20 ms (micro-batch) with a hard per-request SLO deadline of 250 ms for non-stream responses.
- Max batch size: 128 (adaptive, the runtime scales effective batch size based on observed concurrency).
- Streaming mode: enable hybrid streaming (emit tokens as generated from the first available micro-batch). This keeps per-token latency close to raw generation latency while still gaining batching efficiency for compute-heavy steps (KV ops).
- Prefix/KV cache: TTL 15 minutes for session templates; cache hit expected to reduce compute by ~30–50% depending on prompt reuse — please indicate if you have strong prefix reuse across users.
- Quantization profile: start with Q4_0 for the 13B variant for throughput endpoints. For the 70B quality tier, use Q8_dynamic or float16 if quality regression observed. We'll run evals on a representative sample to validate quality delta.
- Model routing: split traffic by route/intent — ~85% -> 13B-Q4_0, 10% -> 70B-Q8 (fallback on quality triggers), 5% -> on-demand 70B float16. We'll tune after perf run.
- Autoscale: min replicas sized for baseline concurrency (~60) with a small burst reserve pool to handle spikes to 200. Add a warm-up policy to keep at least one hot replica per AZ to bound cold start to <100 ms where possible.

What I need from you (Alex) for an accurate perf run:
- 1,000 representative requests (sanitized).
- 2-hour trace with timestamps and concurrency profile OR a synthetic period that reproduces your spike curve.
- A small eval set (50–100 requests) where you can label acceptable vs unacceptable outputs to validate quantization impact.

I'll draft a perf test plan and a short runbook (commands + expected metrics) and share early tomorrow. Also attaching a perf-run template and some example config snippets (see perf link).

Attachments (referenced): perf_run_template.md, config-snippets.txt
